title: What Just Happened
full_review:
In the long tradition of movies that aim to give an insider look at Hollywood -- "A Star is Born" and "The Bad and the Beautiful" among them -- comes the perceptive, if only sporadically funny, comedy "What Just Happened" (Magnolia).

Based on Art Linson's memoir, the fictionalized screenplay (by Linson) centers on beleaguered producer Sam (Robert De Niro), who deftly manages to juggle a host of professional and personal headaches.

First, he needs to salvage his latest film, the violently artsy "Fiercely" starring Sean Penn (as himself). The film has bombed in a preview screening, and studio chief Lou (Catherine Keener) is demanding edits before the film is unveiled at the Cannes Film Festival. (Michael Wincott is a hoot as the druggie British director who must re-cut the film so a dog doesn't perish in the final frames.)

On another front, Sam must convince star Bruce Willis to shave a bushy beard before filming begins on his next movie. If the beard doesn't go, the studio will drop out. Willis sends up his image outrageously, particularly in an explosive F-word-laden tantrum sparked by the beard request.

After that, Sam leans heavily on Willis' nebbishy agent Dick (John Turturro) -- who lives in quivering fear of his own clients -- to convince Willis to shave.

All the while, Sam is hoping to reconcile with wife Kelly (Robin Wright Penn), and he resists the efforts of their divorce counselor to keep them apart. He's further disturbed when he learns Kelly might be having a fling with his screenwriter buddy, Scott (Stanley Tucci). And he's mortified to discover that his teenage daughter, Zoe (Kristen Stewart), may not be the sheltered girl he imagined.

Much of the trenchant humor in director Barry Levinson's satire works, though not all the jokes land. But there's pleasure in watching the performances, while De Niro -- in one of his best recent roles -- manages to convey a sympathetic portrait of an overextended power player in the throes of midlife crisis.

The film contains much rough language and some profanity, crude expressions, brief violent images with gore, an implied nonmarital sexual encounter and a drug reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
